stem: A database administrator proposes a schema change to the billing database. The finance director relies on its reports, the application team maintains the service that reads it, and the IT service manager chairs the change advisory board. What is the system owner's accountability in this change?

options.text: Confirming the change suits the asset they are accountable for
options.why: Ownership is accountability for the asset itself. The owner speaks for the system's purpose, its classification and its acceptable risk, whoever carries out the work. Remember: the owner answers for the asset; the approver signs off on the change.

options.text: Implementing the change inside the maintenance window itself
options.why: That is the implementer's job. An owner who implements their own change has removed the separation the process exists to create.

options.text: Chairing the change advisory board and granting final approval
options.why: Approval is a separate role, usually CAB or a defined delegate. An owner approving their own request is the conflict the board is there to prevent.

options.text: Being consulted as an affected party and informed of the outcome
options.why: That describes a stakeholder. The finance director is a stakeholder here; the owner carries accountability rather than interest.

stem: A change will restart an authentication service for roughly two minutes. Three teams run applications that depend on it. In change management terms, what are those three teams?

options.text: Stakeholders, consulted before the change and informed of the window
options.why: A stakeholder is anyone the change affects. Identifying them is the output of impact analysis, and missing one is how a routine change becomes an unannounced outage. Remember: stakeholders are affected by the change; the owner is accountable for the asset.

options.text: Owners, because their applications stop working during the restart
options.why: They own their own applications, not the authentication service being changed. Being affected does not transfer ownership of the thing being altered.

options.text: Approvers, since the change cannot proceed without their agreement
options.why: Consultation is not a veto. Approval sits with the defined approver, who weighs the stakeholder input and decides.

options.text: Implementers, because they must restart their applications afterwards
options.why: They may have work to do, but the implementer is the party executing this change, not everyone reacting to it.

stem: A change updates a single line in a web server configuration file. The change is classed as low risk. The configuration only takes effect when the web service is restarted, and a payment integration holds long-lived sessions to that service. What is the correct reading of the impact?

options.text: The restart causes downtime, so the dependent integration is in scope whatever the risk class
options.why: Risk and impact are separate judgments. A low risk change is unlikely to go wrong; it can still stop a dependent service dead while it takes effect.

options.text: The impact is negligible because only one line of configuration changed in the file
options.why: Impact is measured by what stops and what depends on it, not by the size of the edit. This is the most common error when judging impact.

options.text: There is no downtime because the server itself is not being rebooted at any point
options.why: A service restart and an application restart both drop sessions without any host reboot. The machine staying up is not the same as the service staying up.

options.text: The payment integration will reconnect automatically, so it is not a stakeholder here
options.why: It may well reconnect, and it may also fail mid-transaction. A dependency you have not asked about is an assumption, not an analysis.

stem: A required operating system update must be applied to a server that also runs a legacy application. The vendor went out of business in 2019, there is no test environment, and no one currently employed has ever reinstalled it. Which element of change management most directly addresses this?

options.text: A verified backout plan: with no vendor or tests, being able to undo is the control
options.why: When you cannot prove it will work beforehand, the control that remains is proving you can undo it. Verified means the restore has actually been tested, not merely written down.

options.text: A longer maintenance window, so there is time to fix problems as they appear in the change
options.why: Time does not substitute for a recovery path. Improvising a repair on an unsupported application inside a window is how a change becomes a multi-day incident.

options.text: Stakeholder notification, so that affected users know the application may well break
options.why: Necessary, but it manages expectations rather than risk. Telling people it might break is not a plan for when it does.

options.text: Recording the legacy application on the deny list so that it can never be updated at all
options.why: Allow and deny lists govern what software may run, not which changes may proceed. The OS update is still required for the host.

stem: During an approved window to replace a failed disk, the engineer notices the server's firmware is several versions behind and updates it as well, since the system is already offline. The firmware update succeeds. What is the problem?

options.text: The firmware update was outside the approved scope and was never assessed or approved
options.why: Approval covers a specific scope. Anything outside it is unauthorized regardless of outcome, because nobody assessed it, nobody can predict its interactions, and the backout plan does not cover it.

options.text: There is no problem, because the work was inside an approved window and succeeded
options.why: The window authorizes a time, not an activity. Success is luck here, and the next time the extra work fails there is no plan for it.

options.text: The engineer should have updated the firmware first, then replaced the disk
options.why: Ordering is irrelevant. The firmware update was not authorized in either position.

options.text: The change should have been classed as standard rather than normal
options.why: A standard change is pre-approved because it is routine and well understood. Adding unassessed firmware work is the opposite of that.

stem: An organization applies monthly workstation patches the same way every month, with a documented procedure, known impact and an established backout. It wants to stop routing each month through the full approval cycle. What is the appropriate mechanism?

options.text: Make it a standard change under a standard operating procedure, pre-approved within that procedure
options.why: Standard changes exist exactly for repeatable, well understood, low risk work. The pre-approval is conditional: step outside the SOP and it is a normal change again.

options.text: Skip change management for patching, since patching reduces risk rather than adding to it
options.why: Patches cause outages routinely. Nothing is exempt from change control for being well intentioned.

options.text: Add the patch management tool to the application allow list so that it may always run
options.why: An allow list governs which software may execute on a host. It has no bearing on whether a change is authorized.

options.text: Have the implementer approve their own changes once a documented procedure exists
options.why: That removes the separation of duties. A standard change is pre-approved by the board, which is not the same as the engineer approving themselves.

stem: Six months after a firewall was replaced and the screened subnet was re-addressed, an incident response team loses two hours working from a network diagram that still shows the old topology. Which change management failure does this illustrate?

options.text: Diagrams were not updated as part of completing the change
options.why: Documentation belongs inside change management for this reason. A diagram that disagrees with reality costs most at exactly the moment you can least afford it.

options.text: The change was implemented outside an approved maintenance window
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests that, and it would not have produced this outcome. The change worked; the record of it did not keep up.

options.text: Impact analysis failed to identify the incident response team as a stakeholder
options.why: Tempting, but the team did not need consulting at the time. What they needed was the artefact to be correct afterwards.

options.text: No backout plan was prepared for the firewall replacement
options.why: A backout covers the change going wrong. This change went right, and the documentation did not follow it.

stem: A team keeps infrastructure configuration in a version control system, with every change committed and reviewed before it is applied. Beyond collaboration, what is the primary security benefit?

options.text: An auditable record of who changed what, and a backout that is a known good commit
options.why: Version control turns rollback from a memory exercise into a checkout, and turns 'who changed this' from an investigation into a query.

options.text: It prevents unauthorized changes from ever being applied to the production systems
options.why: It records and reviews changes; it does not by itself stop someone editing a box directly. That enforcement comes from access control and drift detection.

options.text: It removes the need for a separate approval process for changes to the configuration
options.why: A pull request review can carry the approval, but the approval still has to happen and still has to be someone other than the author.

options.text: It guarantees the configuration in production matches the repository at all times
options.why: Only if something enforces it. Without drift detection the repository can describe a system that no longer exists.

stem: A change moves the organization from VPN-based remote access to a zero trust broker. The technology is deployed and working. Staff continue to follow the old remote access procedure and raise tickets when it fails. What was missed?

options.text: Policies and procedures were not updated for the new system
options.why: When a change alters how people are supposed to work, the written procedure is part of the change. Leaving it stale guarantees the help desk absorbs the difference.

options.text: The change lacked a maintenance window
options.why: The deployment itself succeeded. The gap is downstream of implementation.

options.text: Version control was not applied to the broker configuration
options.why: Good practice, but it would not have told a single user which procedure to follow.

options.text: The old VPN should have been left running indefinitely
options.why: Running both keeps the weaker path open, which defeats the purpose of the change.

stem: A change request proposes upgrading the central LDAP directory. Which TWO items belong in the impact analysis specifically because of technical implications rather than process? (Choose two.)

options.text: Every application that authenticates against the directory and fails during the restart
options.why: Dependencies are the core technical implication: the directory's outage becomes an outage everywhere that trusts it.

options.text: A legacy application known to use an LDAP bind the new version removes
options.why: Legacy applications are called out separately because they often depend on behavior the upgrade drops, and there is rarely a vendor to ask.

options.text: Which member of the change advisory board will chair the review meeting
options.why: That is process and governance, not a technical implication of the change.

options.text: Whether the change request was submitted on the correct form for review
options.why: Administrative compliance, with no bearing on what the change will disturb.

options.text: The date on which the network diagram was last reviewed by the team
options.why: Diagrams matter, but updating them is a completion activity rather than an implication to assess beforehand.

stem: A firmware update was applied to the core switch. It failed, the switch would not boot, and the team had no way to return to the previous version. Which change management element was missing?

options.text: A backout plan
options.why: A backout plan defines, in advance, exactly how to return to the previous known good state when a change fails.

options.text: An impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis identifies what the change will affect. Here the effect was understood; the failure was the inability to undo it.

options.text: A maintenance window
options.why: A maintenance window governs when the change may be applied, not how to recover from it.

options.text: An approval process
options.why: Nothing suggests the change was unauthorised. Approval would not have made it reversible.

stem: An engineer applied an urgent patch to the payments platform at 11am on the busiest trading day of the quarter, causing a 20 minute outage. The patch itself worked correctly. Which element failed?

options.text: The maintenance window
options.why: The change was technically sound and was applied at a time the business could not absorb the disruption.

options.text: The backout plan for the patch
options.why: There was nothing to back out. The patch succeeded; the timing was the failure.

options.text: Testing of the patch
options.why: The patch worked correctly, so testing is not implicated.

options.text: Version control of the patch
options.why: Version control tracks what changed. It does not govern when changes are applied.

stem: A change to the email gateway's filtering rules was approved, tested and applied in the agreed window, and could have been rolled back at any time. Nobody had realised the same gateway also relays alerts from the monitoring system, which stopped arriving for a day. Which element of change management was inadequate?

options.text: The backout plan
options.why: The change could have been undone at any time. The problem was that nobody knew it needed undoing.

options.text: The maintenance window
options.why: The change was applied in the agreed window. Timing was not the failure.

options.text: The approval process
options.why: It was approved. Approval cannot catch a dependency nobody had identified.

options.text: The impact analysis
options.why: An unforeseen side effect on something else is what impact analysis exists to find before the change, not after.

stem: A vendor patch for the VPN gateway is being actively exploited in the wild. The next scheduled change advisory board meeting is in five days. The security manager wants the patch applied tonight. Which approach keeps change management intact while still acting quickly?

options.text: Skip the change process, because an active exploit overrides it and a record can be written next week
options.why: An emergency does not remove the need for control. An unrecorded change to the gateway is exactly the kind that nobody can reverse or explain afterwards.

options.text: Wait for the scheduled meeting, because only the full board may approve any change to a production security device
options.why: Most processes provide an expedited path for this. Five days of known exploitation is a larger risk than the change, and a rigid rule here would be the process causing harm.

options.text: Let the engineer who will apply the patch approve it, since they understand the system best
options.why: Approval by the implementer removes the separation the process exists to create, even when time is short.

options.text: Use the emergency path: a delegate approves, analysis and backout stay, the board reviews later
options.why: Speed changes who approves and how quickly, not whether analysis and a way back exist. The after-the-fact review keeps the board informed and accountable.

stem: A change request to upgrade a database engine includes test results showing a clean pass. The tests were run on a development server with a different operating system build, a tenth of the production data volume and none of the production integrations. The approver is asked to sign. What is the best response?

options.text: Approve, because a passing test result is the evidence the process asks for and the backout plan covers anything that goes wrong
options.why: A test only supports a change to the extent that the test environment resembles production. A backout plan limits the damage but does not replace understanding the impact.

options.text: Approve, but ask the implementer to repeat the same tests in production during the window
options.why: Testing for the first time in production turns the window into the test. It carries the risk the test results were meant to remove.

options.text: Return it to the owner to approve instead, because test results are for the system owner and not for the approver
options.why: Reviewing the evidence is part of approving. Handing the question to another role does not answer whether the evidence is relevant.

options.text: Withhold approval until the tests are production-like, or the gaps are recorded in the impact analysis with a stronger backout
options.why: The weakness is the gap between test and production. Either close the gap or record what remains unknown and plan for it before approving.

stem: A schema change will be applied to a production database during a maintenance window. Which TWO characteristics make the backout plan adequate? (Choose two.)

options.text: It has been rehearsed on a copy of the database, so the time and steps to return are known
options.why: A backout plan that has never been run is a hypothesis. Rehearsal turns it into a known duration and a known sequence.

options.text: It says to restore from the nightly backup, with no check of how long a restore takes
options.why: An untested restore may not fit inside the window and loses everything written since the backup ran. It is a wish, not a plan.

options.text: It names a decision point after which the change is reversed if validation has not passed
options.why: Without a decision point, troubleshooting runs on until the window has gone and no time is left to reverse safely.

options.text: It is written by the approver after the change, once the outcome is known
options.why: A backout plan exists before the change so that it can be judged during approval. Written afterwards it is a report.

options.text: It lists the vendor's support number as the way to recover if the change fails
options.why: Calling a vendor is not a way back to the previous state. It may be useful, but it does not make a plan.

stem: A change needs about three hours of downtime to complete and validate. The only agreed window is Sunday 02:00 to 04:00. The engineer proposes starting at 02:00 and finishing by 05:00, because nobody uses the system overnight. The backout takes ninety minutes. What is the best response?

options.text: Proceed as proposed, because downtime outside business hours does not need stakeholder agreement
options.why: The window is an agreement with the stakeholders, not only a time with low traffic. Overrunning it breaks that agreement and may collide with other jobs.

options.text: Do not start as planned: size the window for change, validation and backout, or agree an extension
options.why: A window sized only for the happy path leaves no time to reverse a failure before users return. Size it for the worst case that must still end cleanly.

options.text: Proceed, and request approval for the overrun afterwards if the change takes longer than expected
options.why: Approval after the fact is not approval. It leaves the stakeholders to discover the outage and removes the choice to refuse it.

options.text: Proceed, but skip validation to fit in the window and validate after users return
options.why: Skipping validation removes the only check that tells the engineer whether to back out. It trades a planned outage for an unplanned one.

stem: One web service on a server hosts twelve applications. A configuration change affects only one of them. The engineer notes that the change takes effect after either restarting that application or restarting the whole web service. Which statement should the impact analysis make?

options.text: Both options cause the same downtime, so the choice does not matter to the impact analysis
options.why: The scope of an interruption is part of the impact. Restarting the service stops every application it hosts, not just the one being changed.

options.text: Restarting the application is always acceptable without a window, because an application restart is not downtime
options.why: An application restart is still downtime for that application's users and for anything holding sessions to it. It is narrower, not free.

options.text: A restart of the application hits one application; a restart of the service hits all twelve, so prefer the narrower
options.why: Impact analysis should name what is interrupted. The smaller scope reduces who must be consulted and how long the window needs to be.

options.text: Restarting the service is safer, because a clean restart of everything removes any unexpected state
options.why: More restarted is more impact, not more safety. Eleven unrelated applications would be interrupted for a change that did not concern them.

stem: Firewall configuration is kept in a repository and deployed from it each night. An engineer fixes an urgent fault by editing the live firewall directly, which opens a port. The next night's deployment overwrites the edit and the fault returns. Which practice would have prevented the problem?

options.text: Make the repository the only route for changes, and alert on drift from it
options.why: A change made outside the repository is invisible to the process that owns the configuration. Making the repository the only route, with drift detection, closes the gap.

options.text: Stop the automated deployment so that only manual changes reach the device
options.why: Automation was not the cause. A manual-only process is the one that allows an edit nobody else can see.

options.text: Update the network diagram after each emergency edit made to the firewall
options.why: A diagram describes the network, but it does not control what is deployed. It would document the drift, not prevent it.

options.text: Add the engineer to the approving group, so that urgent edits are pre-approved
options.why: Pre-approval of the person does not put the change in the repository, so the overwrite would happen anyway. It also weakens separation of roles.

stem: On the same day the change manager receives two requests: add a vendor's remote support tool to the endpoint application allow list for 3,000 laptops, and add a newly reported malicious domain to the web proxy deny list. Which statement best describes how they should be handled?

options.text: Both should receive the same full review, because every list entry changes a production security control
options.why: Treating a routine blocking entry like an expansion of what may run is how a process becomes too slow to use, and people then bypass it.

options.text: Typically the allow list request deserves closer review because it widens what may run; the deny list entry can follow a standard procedure
options.why: Adding to an allow list expands exposure and compatibility risk. Blocking a known-bad domain narrows it, so it suits a standard change with a record.

options.text: Neither needs a change record, because lists are data rather than configuration
options.why: A list entry decides what runs or is reachable. A wrong entry can break an application or open a path, so it is a change.

options.text: The deny list request needs the closer review, because blocking can cut off users, and allow lists only ever make things safer
options.why: An allow list is a restriction on the default, but each entry is an exception to it and widens what is permitted.

stem: A change was approved four months ago, but its schedule slipped. Since then another approved change replaced the load balancer in front of the target system. The engineer wants to proceed tonight under the original approval, saying nothing in the request has changed. What is the right action?

options.text: Proceed, because an approved change stays approved until the change record is closed out
options.why: Approval is given for the system as it was assessed. When the system has changed, the analysis the approval rested on may no longer hold.

options.text: Proceed, and notify the stakeholders so that they are informed of the new date for the work
options.why: Stakeholders are consulted and informed, but they do not approve. Telling them does not renew an approval whose basis has moved.

options.text: Return it for a refreshed impact analysis including the new load balancer, with approver confirmation
options.why: The load balancer changed the dependencies. A fresh analysis and a new approval keep the sequence of analysis, approval, then implementation.

options.text: Ask the system owner to confirm verbally that the old approval still stands for this change
options.why: The owner is accountable for the asset but is not the approving authority. A verbal confirmation also leaves no record.

stem: On the same night two changes are applied. One migrates the internal DNS service to new servers and changes its addresses. The other renews the certificate on an application server that reaches its database by DNS name. Each change was approved and tested separately. The application fails after both are applied. Which element of change management was inadequate?

options.text: The backout plan, because the second change should have been reversed
options.why: A backout may well have been available, but the failure was not that a change could not be undone. It was that nobody saw the two interacting.

options.text: The standard operating procedure, because the certificate renewal should have been a standard change
options.why: A standard change would have skipped analysis altogether, which makes it less likely that the interaction is noticed.

options.text: The stakeholder notification, because the application team was not told about either change
options.why: Telling people helps them prepare, but it would not have exposed the dependency between two changes.

options.text: The impact analysis, because it examined each change alone and ignored dependencies between them
options.why: Dependencies include other changes. A combined view of the change calendar for the window would have shown that one change alters what the other relies on.

stem: A change disables TLS 1.0 on all internal servers to meet a new standard. Lab test results show every modern application working. A finance application written years ago, which the vendor no longer supports, is not in the lab and is known to require TLS 1.0. What is the best next step?

options.text: Proceed, because the test results show success and the standard requires the change to be made
options.why: The test results say nothing about an application that was not tested. The standard sets the goal but does not remove the need to know what will break.

options.text: Treat the legacy application as a known dependency; test it or agree a recorded, time-limited exception first
options.why: A legacy system that cannot be updated is a known dependency that testing missed. It must be assessed and either protected or excepted in a way that is recorded.

options.text: Disable TLS 1.0 only on the servers the finance application does not use, and do not record the reason
options.why: Leaving it hidden means the exposure continues with no record, and the standard is silently not met.

options.text: Ask the finance team to approve the change, since they are the affected stakeholders in this case
options.why: Stakeholders are consulted, but their agreement does not tell anyone whether the application will work, and it does not create the missing test.

stem: A new subnet is added for IoT cameras, with its own firewall rules, and the change is working. Which TWO items must be updated to complete the change? (Choose two.)

options.text: The network diagram, so responders can see the new segment and what it may reach
options.why: A diagram that does not show the new subnet misleads anyone using it during an incident.

options.text: The previous year's audit report, so that it reflects the new subnet
options.why: An audit report records a past finding. It is not changed because the environment changed later.

options.text: The configuration repository, so the committed firewall rules match what is running
options.why: If the repository and the device disagree, the next deployment can undo the change or the next engineer can be misled.

options.text: The vendor's marketing material for the cameras
options.why: Not part of the organization's change record, and it plays no role in operating or securing the network.

options.text: The approver's job description, so that it lists the new subnet
options.why: Approval roles are defined in the process, not in a list of subnets. This confuses who approves with what was changed.

stem: During a firewall upgrade the engineer finds that 80 percent of validation tests pass, but the VPN does not. The approved plan says to back out at 03:30 if validation has not passed. It is 03:20, and the engineer believes thirty more minutes of troubleshooting will fix it. The window closes at 04:00. What should the engineer do?

options.text: Keep troubleshooting to 04:00, because most of the change works and backing out would waste the effort
options.why: Sunk effort is not a reason to continue. The decision point was set to protect the window while there was still time to reverse safely.

options.text: Stop at the decision point and back out, unless the approver agrees to change the plan
options.why: The plan exists to take this decision out of the moment. Extending it is a change to the approved plan and belongs to the approver, not the implementer.

options.text: Apply a different fix the engineer thinks is more likely to work, since the firewall is already open for changes
options.why: Any step outside the approved scope is a restricted activity. Being in the window does not widen what was authorized.

options.text: Continue and tell the stakeholders that the VPN is delayed, since they are the ones who will be affected
options.why: Informing stakeholders is right, but it does not give the implementer the authority to overrun the plan. The approver decides that.
